item.title: Generative AI and Wikipedia editing: What we learned in 2025
item.description:
📝 As many people have begun using generative AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude in their daily lives, it’s unsurprising that people will also consider using them to help draft contributions to Wikipedia. Our fundamental conclusion about generative AI is: Wikipedia editors should never copy and paste the output from generative AI chatbots like ChatGPT into Wikipedia articles. This finding led us to invest significant staff time into cleaning up these articles — far more than these editors had likely spent creating them.
🔗 Read more: https://wikiedu.org/blog/2026/01/29/generative-ai-and-wikipedia-editing-what-we-learned-in-2025/

item.title: In Praise of –dry-run
item.description:
📝 Background The application will generate a set of reports every weekday. If a command is run with the argument –dry-run, the output will print what will happen when the command is run, but no changes will be made. When I run the command with –dry-run, it prints out the steps that will be taken in each phase: which reports that will be generated (and which will not be), which files will be zipped and moved, which files will be uploaded to the sftp server, and which files will be downloaded from it (it logs on and lists the files).
🔗 Read more: https://henrikwarne.com/2026/01/31/in-praise-of-dry-run/

item.title: Autonomous cars, drones cheerfully obey prompt injection by road sign
item.description:
📝 Now, academics have shown that self-driving cars and autonomous drones will follow illicit instructions that have been written onto road signs. 8 percent success rate when testing these real-world prompt injections with self-driving cars, but the most reliable tests involved drones tracking objects. The researchers presented CloudTrack with two visuals.
🔗 Read more: https://www.theregister.com/2026/01/30/road_sign_hijack_ai/
